system:
You are the analysis agent of a reporting platform for Australia's threatened species. Conservation practitioners — people in government agencies, NGOs and recovery teams who decide where to survey, what to protect and what to escalate — read what you produce. You have read-only SQL access to the platform's database and produce insights from it, each grounded in queries you ran.

# The data

PostgreSQL 17 with PostGIS 3.5. The corpus is every occurrence record the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA) tags as nationally threatened (EPBC Critically Endangered, Endangered or Vulnerable), observed January 2015 to 2026-09-30, from one bulk download (DOI 10.26197/ala.40eee344-07ce-48d2-9ec2-be39574ff4c7): about 2.1 million records, 1,850 taxa, 300+ contributing datasets. Alongside it are all-taxa effort counts per 0.1° cell per month for the same period.

corpus.analysable_occurrences — VIEW — the records to analyse: occurrences that are valid, dated, and not from telemetry (animal-tracking) datasets. Includes population ('wild' or 'managed' — managed means a fenced haven, reintroduction or other managed population, set from the dataset or from corpus.managed_populations) and dataset_kind (the dataset's own kind). Prefer this over occurrences.
  columns: record_id text, source text, source_record_id text, occurrence_id text, harvest_id text, snapshot_page text, fetched_at timestamp with time zone, data_resource_uid text, license text, taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, national_status text, event_date timestamp with time zone, first_loaded_at timestamp with time zone, decimal_latitude double precision, decimal_longitude double precision, coordinate_uncertainty_m double precision, state_province text, ibra_region text, locality text, geom USER-DEFINED, basis_of_record text, individual_count integer, recorded_by_pseudonym text, occurrence_remarks text, event_remarks text, source_assertions ARRAY, is_valid boolean, issue_count integer, cell_lat numeric, cell_lon numeric, event_day date, managed_by_rule boolean, dataset_kind text, population text

corpus.datasets — TABLE — contributing datasets; kind is 'wild', 'managed' (fenced havens, reintroductions) or 'telemetry' (excluded from analysable_occurrences).
  columns: data_resource_uid text, name text, kind text, kind_reason text, first_seen_at timestamp with time zone

corpus.effort_cells — TABLE — ALL-taxa record counts (threatened or not, telemetry excluded) per 0.1° cell per month: the denominator for reporting rates. Join on cell_lat/cell_lon and month.
  columns: cell_lat numeric, cell_lon numeric, period_start date, period_end date, records integer, harvest_id text

corpus.harvest_runs — TABLE — provenance of each harvest (the corpus download and the effort counts).
  columns: harvest_id text, harvest_key text, run_id text, source text, description text, query jsonb, started_at timestamp with time zone, finished_at timestamp with time zone, expected_records integer, retrieved_records integer, complete boolean, corpus_hash text, request_count integer, warnings jsonb, analysis jsonb, loaded_at timestamp with time zone

corpus.managed_populations — TABLE — curated rules marking managed populations: a taxon in a state (optionally narrowed to an IBRA region and a dataset), e.g. Bilby in NSW, where it survives only in fenced havens, or Woylie in AWC's Mt Gibson haven. Already applied in analysable_occurrences.population.
  columns: taxon_concept_id text, state_province text, note text, rule_id integer, ibra_region text, data_resource_uid text

corpus.occurrences — TABLE — every canonical occurrence record, telemetry included. event_date is the observation instant (timestamptz); event_day is its Australian Eastern local date. geom is a PostGIS Point (SRID 4326); cell_lat/cell_lon are the 0.1° grid cell (rounded to nearest, as ALA assigns them).
  columns: record_id text, source text, source_record_id text, occurrence_id text, harvest_id text, snapshot_page text, fetched_at timestamp with time zone, data_resource_uid text, license text, taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, national_status text, event_date timestamp with time zone, first_loaded_at timestamp with time zone, decimal_latitude double precision, decimal_longitude double precision, coordinate_uncertainty_m double precision, state_province text, ibra_region text, locality text, geom USER-DEFINED, basis_of_record text, individual_count integer, recorded_by_pseudonym text, occurrence_remarks text, event_remarks text, source_assertions ARRAY, is_valid boolean, issue_count integer, cell_lat numeric, cell_lon numeric, event_day date, managed_by_rule boolean

corpus.taxa — TABLE — one row per taxon (key taxon_concept_id); national_status is the EPBC status ALA attached.
  columns: taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, taxon_rank text, kingdom text, phylum text, taxon_class text, taxon_order text, family text, genus text, national_status text, status_seen_at timestamp with time zone

corpus.taxon_tiers — VIEW — per taxon: analysable records since 2015, last_record_day, and statistical_tier (≥100 records since 2015).
  columns: taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, national_status text, records_since_2015 bigint, last_record_day date, statistical_tier boolean

Useful facts: EPSG:3577 (Australian Albers, equal-area, metres) is available for gridding and areas; ibra_region is the IBRA 7 bioregion (null offshore — IBRA covers land only); coordinate_uncertainty_m is the radius the true position may lie within.

**Dates: use event_day** (the Australian Eastern local date) for every date window, count by period and date you report — not event_date, which is an instant stored in UTC and would put early-morning Australian records on the previous day.

# Known properties of this data — read before interpreting anything

- **Records measure effort as much as animals.** These are mostly opportunistic records. All-taxa recording roughly doubled between 2017–19 and 2022–24 (about 1.9×), so counts and range measures grow with effort. Use corpus.effort_cells as a denominator where it matters.
- **Recent months are incomplete.** Datasets reach ALA months to a year late: January–August 2026 holds about 20% of the records January–August 2024 holds, and eBird (the largest dataset) has not loaded 2026 at all. A recent decline is not evidence of anything until this is accounted for.
- **Sources start and stop.** A compilation that ends in 2020, or a targeted survey wound up inside an ongoing state atlas, looks exactly like range loss. Check which datasets carry a taxon's records in each period before calling a change real.
- **Locations vary in precision.** About half the analysable records are located to within 2 km; about a third state no uncertainty; ALA generalises many sensitive species to roughly 10 km.
- **Managed populations** (population = 'managed': fenced havens, reintroductions) are in the analysable view and are not wild trend.
- **National status** is as ALA attached it. Never infer, change or second-guess a taxon's conservation status.
- Taxonomy can shift: a taxon "disappearing" from a region can be a name re-assignment.

# How to work

- Call run_sql with one SELECT (or WITH … SELECT) per call, no trailing statements. Results are capped at 200 rows and queries time out after 30 s, so aggregate in SQL rather than pulling rows. Each call returns a query_id.
- Record each insight with record_insight as soon as it is established. Every insight cites the query_ids whose results support it, and every number in it must be a value those queries returned or simple arithmetic on them. Do not state figures you did not query.
- taxon_concept_id must be copied exactly from corpus.taxa; when an insight is about several taxa, put the main one there (or null) and list the others in related_taxa; region is an IBRA region name exactly as in ibra_region, or null for a national insight; period_start and period_end are the window the insight describes.
- Say how confident you are and why, in the confidence field: record counts, the datasets involved, effort, precision, and any artefact that could explain the pattern.
- When you have recorded everything worth recording, stop.

tools.name: run_sql
tools.description: Run one read-only SQL query (a single SELECT or WITH … SELECT) against the corpus. Returns a query_id, the columns and up to 200 rows. Cite the query_id in any insight that relies on the result.

sql.description: One SELECT or WITH … SELECT statement.

purpose.description: One line: what this query is for.

tools.name: record_insight
tools.description: Record one insight. Every figure must come from the cited queries.

category.description: A short label of your own for the kind of insight.

taxon_concept_id.description: Exactly as in corpus.taxa, or null for a non-taxon insight.

related_taxa.description: Optional: other taxon_concept_ids this insight is about, exactly as in corpus.taxa.

region.description: IBRA region name exactly as in ibra_region, or null for national.

period_start.description: YYYY-MM-DD — start of the window the insight describes.

figures.description: The numbers behind the insight, as returned by your queries.

confidence.description: Why this should or should not be trusted: records, datasets, effort, precision, possible artefacts.

summary.description: One or two sentences a practitioner can act on.

query_ids.description: The run_sql query_ids whose results support this insight.

messages.content:
It is October 2026. A conservation practitioner responsible for Australia's threatened species asks: from this data, what should I know right now — what has changed, what is concerning, what is new, and where are we blind?

Investigate as you judge best and record each insight worth their attention — aim for the most important 20 to 40. For each, be explicit about confidence and about any data artefact that could explain the pattern.

input.sql: SELECT extract(year from event_day)::int yr, count(*) recs, count(distinct taxon_concept_id) taxa, count(distinct data_resource_uid) ds, sum(case when population='managed' then 1 else 0 end) managed FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
input.purpose: Yearly overview of analysable records, taxa, datasets

input.sql: SELECT extract(year from period_start)::int yr, sum(records) recs, count(distinct (cell_lat,cell_lon)) cells FROM corpus.effort_cells GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
input.purpose: All-taxa effort per year

input.sql: SELECT o.data_resource_uid, d.name, d.kind, count(*) recs, min(event_day) first_day, max(event_day) last_day, count(distinct taxon_concept_id) taxa, sum(case when event_day>='2025-01-01' then 1 else 0 end) recs_2025plus FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences o LEFT JOIN corpus.datasets d USING (data_resource_uid) GROUP BY 1,2,3 ORDER BY recs DESC LIMIT 40
input.purpose: Largest datasets with temporal coverage

input.sql: SELECT coalesce(state_province,'(none)') st, count(*) recs, sum(case when event_day between '2022-01-01' and '2024-12-31' then 1 else 0 end) r22_24, sum(case when event_day>='2025-01-01' then 1 else 0 end) r25plus, count(distinct taxon_concept_id) taxa, sum(case when population='managed' then 1 else 0 end) managed FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC
input.purpose: Records by state

input.sql: SELECT d.data_resource_uid, d.name, d.kind, d.kind_reason, count(o.record_id) recs, min(o.event_day), max(o.event_day) FROM corpus.datasets d LEFT JOIN corpus.occurrences o USING (data_resource_uid) WHERE d.kind<>'wild' GROUP BY 1,2,3,4 ORDER BY recs DESC
input.purpose: Managed and telemetry datasets

WITH w AS (
  SELECT taxon_concept_id, cell_lat, cell_lon,
    sum(case when event_day between '2017-01-01' and '2019-12-31' then 1 else 0 end) a,
    sum(case when event_day between '2022-01-01' and '2024-12-31' then 1 else 0 end) b
  FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences WHERE population='wild' AND event_day between '2017-01-01' and '2024-12-31'
  GROUP BY 1,2,3),
e AS (
  SELECT cell_lat, cell_lon,
    sum(case when period_start between '2017-01-01' and '2019-12-31' then records else 0 end) ea,
    sum(case when period_start between '2022-01-01' and '2024-12-31' then records else 0 end) eb
  FROM corpus.effort_cells GROUP BY 1,2),
t AS (
  SELECT w.taxon_concept_id, sum(a) a, sum(b) b, count(*) filter (where a>0) ca, count(*) filter (where b>0) cb,
    sum(ea) ea, sum(eb) eb
  FROM w LEFT JOIN e USING (cell_lat, cell_lon) GROUP BY 1)
SELECT x.vernacular_name, x.scientific_name, x.national_status, a, b, ca, cb, round((b::numeric/nullif(eb,0))/nullif(a::numeric/nullif(ea,0),0),2) rr_ratio, round(eb::numeric/nullif(ea,0),2) eff_ratio, t.taxon_concept_id
FROM t JOIN corpus.taxa x USING (taxon_concept_id)
WHERE a+b >= 150 AND a>=50
ORDER BY rr_ratio ASC LIMIT 60

input.purpose: Recent-month completeness by dataset: Jan-Aug 2024 vs 2025 vs 2026

confidence.basis: Direct counts per dataset by event_day. The shortfall is reporting lag, not biology: eBird has not loaded any 2026 records, and state atlases (VBA, SA Fauna) have loaded under 3% of their Jan–Aug 2024 volume for Jan–Aug 2026. Even 2025 is incomplete: VBA 2,575 vs 7,964 and the all-taxa effort denominator is also down ~20% on 2024.

input.summary: Do not read any 2025–2026 decline in this data as real. eBird has loaded nothing for 2026, and the state atlases hold under 3% of their usual volume. iNaturalist is the only source that has grown, so records from 2026 so far mostly show where iNaturalist users go and which species they photograph. For trends, compare years up to 2024 at the latest, and divide by recording effort.

confidence.basis: Counts of wild analysable records by state and taxonomic class. The pattern comes from which datasets ALA holds: in WA, Tasmania and Queensland since 2022, eBird, iNaturalist and Birdata supply almost all records, and Queensland's WildNet supplies only 589. No WA or Tasmanian government atlas appears among the large contributors. This is a gap in coverage, not a sign that species are absent.

input.summary: Outside NSW, Victoria and SA, this corpus is mostly a bird dataset. Birds make up 94% of wild records in WA, 95% in Tasmania and 85% in Queensland (2022–24). WA, which holds a large share of Australia's threatened plants, has only 954 threatened-plant records in three years, and Tasmania has 342. Absence of records for threatened plants, reptiles, frogs and invertebrates in WA, Tasmania and Queensland says nothing about the species. Before drawing conclusions there, get the state agencies' own data (e.g. DBCA, Natural Values Atlas, WildNet).

confidence.level: high that this is an artefact
confidence.basis: For each taxon, the records that vanish are almost all from Fauna Atlas N.T. (dr361), which stopped delivering after 2022 (last record March 2024). The NESP A12 northern threatened-species compilation (dr23181) ends in 2020. iNaturalist and AWC records continue at low levels. The fall in reporting rate (ratio 0.00–0.07 per unit effort) cannot be read as population loss. Whether these mammals are actually declining is not known from this data.

input.summary: Records of Top End threatened mammals have collapsed since 2020: Northern Brushtail Possum from 6,204 records (2017–19) to 206 (2022–24), Djintamoonga (Black-footed Tree-rat) from 1,726 to 0, and Arnhem Land Rock-rat from 340 to 2. The cause is that the NT Fauna Atlas and the NESP A12 compilation stopped flowing to ALA, not shown population loss. In practice we have no current view of northern mammals, a group known to be declining. Get NT government survey data directly rather than relying on this feed.

WITH w AS (
  SELECT taxon_concept_id, cell_lat, cell_lon,
    sum(case when event_day between '2017-01-01' and '2019-12-31' then 1 else 0 end) a,
    sum(case when event_day between '2022-01-01' and '2024-12-31' then 1 else 0 end) b,
    count(distinct data_resource_uid) nds
  FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences WHERE population='wild' AND event_day between '2017-01-01' and '2024-12-31'
    AND data_resource_uid IN ('dr2009','dr368','dr359','dr1411','dr1097','dr365')
  GROUP BY 1,2,3),
e AS (
  SELECT cell_lat, cell_lon,
    sum(case when period_start between '2017-01-01' and '2019-12-31' then records else 0 end) ea,
    sum(case when period_start between '2022-01-01' and '2024-12-31' then records else 0 end) eb
  FROM corpus.effort_cells GROUP BY 1,2),
t AS (
  SELECT w.taxon_concept_id, sum(a) a, sum(b) b, count(*) filter (where a>0) ca, count(*) filter (where b>0) cb,
    sum(ea) ea, sum(eb) eb
  FROM w LEFT JOIN e USING (cell_lat, cell_lon) GROUP BY 1)
SELECT x.vernacular_name, x.scientific_name, x.taxon_class, x.national_status, a, b, ca, cb, round((b::numeric/nullif(eb,0))/nullif(a::numeric/nullif(ea,0),0),2) rr_ratio, t.taxon_concept_id
FROM t JOIN corpus.taxa x USING (taxon_concept_id)
WHERE a >= 150 AND ca>=10
ORDER BY rr_ratio ASC LIMIT 50

WITH w AS (
  SELECT taxon_concept_id, cell_lat, cell_lon,
    sum(case when event_day between '2017-01-01' and '2019-12-31' then 1 else 0 end) a,
    sum(case when event_day between '2022-01-01' and '2024-12-31' then 1 else 0 end) b
  FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences WHERE population='wild' AND event_day between '2017-01-01' and '2024-12-31'
    AND data_resource_uid IN ('dr2009','dr368','dr359','dr1411','dr1097','dr365')
  GROUP BY 1,2,3),
e AS (
  SELECT cell_lat, cell_lon,
    sum(case when period_start between '2017-01-01' and '2019-12-31' then records else 0 end) ea,
    sum(case when period_start between '2022-01-01' and '2024-12-31' then records else 0 end) eb
  FROM corpus.effort_cells GROUP BY 1,2),
t AS (
  SELECT w.taxon_concept_id, sum(a) a, sum(b) b, sum(ea) ea, sum(eb) eb
  FROM w LEFT JOIN e USING (cell_lat, cell_lon) GROUP BY 1),
r AS (SELECT x.taxon_class, (b::numeric/nullif(eb,0))/nullif(a::numeric/nullif(ea,0),0) rr, b::numeric/a raw FROM t JOIN corpus.taxa x USING (taxon_concept_id) WHERE a>=150)
SELECT taxon_class, count(*) n, round(percentile_cont(0.5) within group (order by rr)::numeric,2) median_rr, round(percentile_cont(0.25) within group (order by rr)::numeric,2) q1, round(percentile_cont(0.75) within group (order by rr)::numeric,2) q3, round(percentile_cont(0.5) within group (order by raw)::numeric,2) median_raw FROM r GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC

WITH tx AS (SELECT taxon_concept_id, vernacular_name FROM corpus.taxa WHERE vernacular_name IN ('Curlew Sandpiper','Lesser Sand Plover','Eastern Curlew','Great Knot','Painted Honeyeater','Latham''s Snipe','Red Knot','Swift Parrot')),

r AS (SELECT o.taxon_concept_id, extract(year from event_day)::int yr, count(*) n FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences o JOIN tx USING (taxon_concept_id) WHERE population='wild' AND event_day between '2015-01-01' and '2024-12-31' AND data_resource_uid IN ('dr2009','dr359') GROUP BY 1,2),
e AS (SELECT c.taxon_concept_id, extract(year from period_start)::int yr, sum(records) eff FROM c JOIN corpus.effort_cells ec USING (cell_lat, cell_lon) WHERE period_start between '2015-01-01' and '2024-12-31' GROUP BY 1,2)

confidence.basis: The signal comes from eBird and Birdata, which ran continuously throughout, and is measured against all-taxa effort in the cells where the species occurs. The reporting rate fell in almost every year, and raw records fell even though effort roughly doubled. Its effort-adjusted ratio of 0.37 is far below the bird median of 0.89. Caveats: sample sizes are small (37–80 records a year). The NT drop (263 to 14) partly reflects the NT Fauna Atlas stopping. Effort growth is concentrated near cities rather than on remote northern flats, which could dilute the rate. Lesser Sand Plover is also easily confused with Greater Sand Plover.

input.summary: Of the threatened shorebirds checked here, Lesser Sand Plover shows the clearest effort-adjusted decline. Its eBird/Birdata reporting rate fell from 22.8 to 3.6 per 100,000 all-taxa records between 2015 and 2024, and records fell outright (80 in 2019, 37 in 2024) while recording effort grew. Ask for targeted shorebird-count data (e.g. Shorebirds 2020 / BirdLife counts) from Queensland and north-west WA to confirm.

confidence.basis: Thousands of eBird and Birdata records a year in each series, measured against all-taxa effort in each species' cells. Curlew Sandpiper's rate dropped by about a third between 2019 and 2020 and has stayed at the lower level, which is consistent but not proof. The cause could be population decline, or the growth in non-shorebird recording near coastal cities (iNaturalist and suburban birding) diluting the denominator. Eastern Curlew is a useful check: its rate is roughly stable, so the dilution is not uniform across species.

input.summary: Curlew Sandpiper (Critically Endangered) has been reported about a third less often per unit of recording effort since 2020: around 160 per 100,000 all-taxa records in 2015–19, against 99–114 in 2020–24. Red Knot drifted down from about 120 to about 85. Eastern Curlew and Great Knot are roughly stable on the same measure. Use this to prioritise Curlew Sandpiper and Red Knot when reviewing structured shorebird counts.

confidence.basis: Hundreds to about a thousand eBird and Birdata records a year, measured against all-taxa effort in the cells where each species occurs. The declines are gradual and sustained rather than step changes, which argues against a single source artefact. Two other woodland species (Diamond Firetail, Southern Whiteface) are stable on the same measure, which argues against pure denominator dilution. Still, effort growth from iNaturalist and peri-urban birding could dilute reporting rates unevenly. Opportunistic records are not counts, so treat this as a flag, not a trend estimate.

input.summary: Two south-eastern woodland birds are reported steadily less often per unit of effort. South-eastern Brown Treecreeper fell from 73–84 per 100,000 all-taxa records (2015–18) to 35 in 2024, and South-eastern Hooded Robin from about 40 (2017–20) to 22 in 2024. Raw records are flat while recording effort roughly doubled. Diamond Firetail and Southern Whiteface hold steady on the same measure. Use structured woodland bird survey data (e.g. Birdata 2-ha surveys) to check these two first.

confidence.basis: The records available are noisy. The 2023–24 eBird surge (574 records in 2024 from only 11 cells) points to repeat visits to a few known sites, so record counts are not useful. The narrowing number of occupied cells is the more informative measure. Captive-bred releases are not flagged as managed in this corpus and may make up some records. State-atlas records (BioNet etc.) fell from 749 to 53 between 2020 and 2024, partly through data flow.

input.summary: Critically Endangered Regent Honeyeater is being reported from fewer places. eBird/Birdata detections came from 21–24 cells in 2017–19 but only 10–11 in 2022–24, and across all continuous sources from 122 cells to 63, even though record numbers rose (574 in 2024). Birders are concentrating on a few sites. Check whether captive-release sites are inflating the counts, and steer surveys towards historical sites with no recent records.

I recorded 30 insights; the full list is above. The most important point first: most of the changes this data shows reflect which datasets do and don't reach ALA, not changes in the species. Each insight states its confidence and the artefacts that could explain it.

**What has changed: the data itself**
- **2025–26 is incomplete.** eBird has loaded nothing for 2026, and the Victorian and SA atlases hold under 3% of their usual volume. iNaturalist is now the largest 2026 source. Trends should stop at 2024.
- **Several state feeds have stopped or are about to.** The NT Fauna Atlas has delivered nothing since March 2024, and Queensland's WildNet fell from 851 records in 2017 to 60 in 2024. FrogID has nothing after November 2024. Wild records in Arnhem Land and the Tiwi Islands fell 81–85% between 2017–19 and 2022–24, while national recording effort roughly doubled.
- **Nearly half of well-recorded taxa hang on one source.** Of the 575 taxa with at least 30 records in 2022–24, 274 get 90% or more of them from one dataset. For 131 of them, 34 Critically Endangered, that dataset is NSW BioNet. If it stalls, those taxa will look as if they have lost range.

**What is concerning (moderate confidence; for verification, not escalation yet)**
These are reporting rates per unit of all-species recording effort, compared with a typical bird ratio of 0.89 (2022–24 against 2017–19).
- **Lesser Sand Plover:** 22.8 records per 100,000 all-species records in 2015, 3.6 in 2024, and raw records fell even as effort grew. Yearly samples are small (37–80 records).
- **Curlew Sandpiper:** down about a third since 2020 and staying there. **Red Knot** drifted down too.
- **South-eastern Brown Treecreeper** (about 80 down to 35) and **South-eastern Hooded Robin** (about 40 down to 22). Other woodland birds, such as Diamond Firetail, hold steady on the same measure.
- **Regent Honeyeater:** reported from about half as many places (122 cells down to 63) even though records rose. Captive releases aren't flagged as managed and may be in the counts.
- **Possible heat die-off of Grey-headed Flying-foxes in SA, 12 January 2026:** 8 of 10 records that day mention death or heat. This rests on keyword matching only, so check with carers and the state agency.

**Apparent declines and recoveries not to escalate on this data**
Each of these turned out to be one survey program starting or stopping:
- Golden Sun Moth, Grey-headed Flying-fox, Southern Right Whale, Gould's Petrel and South-eastern Red-tailed Black-cockatoo.
- The northern mammals: Northern Brushtail Possum, Black-footed Tree-rat and Arnhem Land Rock-rat.
- Southern Bell Frog, which is actually being found in more places.
- Marine turtles.
- The apparent rise of Australasian Bittern.
- Plant record counts: typical plant ratio is 0.27, because plant surveys log individual plants.

**What is new**
- **Newly surveyed plants:** Large-flower Groundsel (2,904 plants, SA), Elusive Bush-pea (405 plants, Sydney Basin) and Lax Leek-orchid. These are new baselines, not trends.
- **A spring 2026 surge of SA spider-orchid records** on iNaturalist.
- **Rare species turning up on iNaturalist:** Bulloak Jewel butterfly (32 records in 2025–26 against 13 in the ten years before), Critically Endangered crayfish, and Kroombit Treefrog.
- **A new Night Parrot record** in the Channel Country (September 2026). The recovery team should be alerted.

**Where you are blind**
- **Outside NSW, Victoria and SA, the data is mostly birds:** 94% of WA records and 95% of Tasmanian ones. WA has only 954 threatened-plant records in three years.
- **178 of 392 Critically Endangered taxa have fewer than 10 records.** Baw Baw Frog's last record is from 2015.
- **Species listed as populations barely appear:** the listed Koala has 8 records and the northern Southern Cassowary population 3.
- **Wild populations of haven species are nearly invisible:** Woylie has no wild record since 2022, and wild Bilbies have a handful of records against 120,668 from NSW havens.
- **Location precision is poor for key species:** every record since 2020 of Carnaby's (Short-billed) Black-cockatoo is blurred to 10 km or more, so none can support site decisions.
- **Many places are no longer recorded at all:** 274 WA cells and 231 Tasmanian cells that had threatened records in 2015–19 had no records of any species in 2022–24.

**Data fixes needed**
- **Probable reintroductions labelled wild:** Plains Rat in the Pilliga region and Red-tailed Phascogale at Mallee Cliffs (NSW) look like reintroductions but are counted as wild. I inferred this from the pattern; the localities haven't been checked.
- **Haven-visitor records counted as wild:** some iNaturalist records inside haven regions slip past the managed-population rules, which are tied to one dataset.
